atoms.text: There are many famous women in history who worked together to achieve great things. Their stories continue to inspire us to this day. But I believe that the story of Mrs Eliza Ruhamah Scidmore and First Lady Helen Herron Taft is an especially remarkable reminder of how far teamwork can bring us, and we should all learn about their story. These two women not only dramatically improved the landscape of our capital city, but also established a tradition of US-Japan diplomacy that would define the countries’ relations for over a century to come.

Neither Mrs Scidmore nor First Lady Taft could have single-handedly designed and realised the picturesque landscape enjoyed in today’s Washington, D.C. Mrs Scidmore, a passionate traveller who had enjoyed many trips to Japan, visualised how beautiful her own country’s capital would look scattered with pink and white blossoms. She tried for over twenty years to gain support for her landscaping dream. Despite her lack of success, she never gave up, and eventually her idea landed in the right hands. Mrs Scidmore had written a letter to the incoming First Lady, Helen Taft, who also loved cherry blossoms, having herself lived in Japan for a few years. The First Lady, excited by this new image of the capital city, immediately put her political connections to use. Within three years, a gift of 3,020 cherry blossom trees had arrived in D.C. from Tokyo. What Mrs Scidmore and First Lady Taft each lacked, they fulfilled in each other with teamwork, and the result is the beautiful city we see today.

She tried for over twenty years to gain support for her landscaping dream. Despite her lack of success, she never gave up, and eventually her idea landed in the right hands. Mrs Scidmore had written a letter to the incoming First Lady, Helen Taft, who also loved cherry blossoms, having herself lived in Japan for a few years. What Mrs Scidmore and First Lady Taft each lacked, they fulfilled in each other with teamwork, and the result is the beautiful city we see today.

atoms.text: Mrs Scidmore and First Lady Taft’s teamwork didn’t only have a local effect on the capital city. These women’s partnership was essential in defining US-Japan diplomatic relations for at least a century to come. Receiving First Lady Taft’s request for cherry trees and wanting to strengthen its relationship with the US, Japan gave the trees as a gift in 1912. First Lady Taft’s husband, President Taft, later sent flowering dogwood trees to Japan as a gift of gratitude for the botanical enrichment of the city. In 1981, a typhoon ravaged much of Japan and destroyed their only specimens of certain types of cherry blossom trees. In a true act of international friendship, the US identified some of these lost species in the healthy trees of Washington, D.C., cut off some branches, and sent them back to Japan so that they could reforest their own cherry trees. Mrs Scidmore and First Lady Taft’s partnership had an even greater effect than they had planned: their work established a tradition of botanic diplomacy with Japan.

atoms.text: The story of Mrs Scidmore and First Lady Taft thus forms a wonderful inspirational tale. The deed of planting the cherry blossoms in Washington D.C. could not have been done by only one of these women. They each brought their own dreams and privileges to the table, and the result was greater than either of them could have imagined.
